analysis.one_liner: Forces public utilities to refund excess deferred taxes to their customers instead of keeping them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: When Congress cut the corporate tax rate in the Tax Reform Act of 1986, utilities had big piles of 'deferred taxes' they had collected from customers under the old, higher rate. A rule called 'normalization' let utilities keep that money and flow it back slowly through their books instead of handing it to customers. This bill repealed that rule, which would have let state regulators return the excess to utility ratepayers through lower bills. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential and business customers of investor-owned electric and gas utilities, who would see the excess deferred tax reserves returned to them through their rates.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 203(e) of the Tax Reform Act of 1986, the provision that extended 'normalization' accounting to excess deferred tax reserves of public utilities.
The bill's stated purpose is to remove the limit that the 1986 act placed on consumers' benefits from the corporate rate reduction's effect on utilities' deferred tax reserves.
Without the normalization requirement, state utility regulators would be free to order the excess deferred taxes returned to ratepayers rather than retained by the utilities.

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric and gas utilities, which would have to give up the excess deferred tax reserves currently held on their books and refund them to customers.

drawbacks.text: Utilities argue that normalization accounting preserves orderly ratemaking and that stripping it would hit the cash flow and earnings of companies that financed system investments on the expectation of keeping those reserves; a sudden mandated refund could pressure utilities' finances.
Refunds would flow unevenly across states, since state regulators would decide how and when to return the reserves, and the bill leaves the mechanics entirely to them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to customers is real and direct: money collected under a repealed higher tax rate goes back to the people who paid it. The cost falls on utility shareholders, who would see reserves they have held since the 1986 rate cut returned to customers. Utilities' objections about financial disruption have force, but the bill simply removes a federal rule that prevented regulators from returning money that came from ratepayers in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Representative Byron Dorgan of North Dakota, joined by Representative Robert Matsui, introduced the Utility Ratepayer Refund Act of 1992 on April 29, 1992.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investor-owned utilities are better off, since they continue holding the excess deferred tax reserves that the bill would have returned to ratepayers. Ratepayers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the normalization rule and return excess deferred taxes to utility customers.

for.name: Robert Matsui
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Investor-owned utility industry
against.role: Public electric and gas utilities holding excess deferred tax reserves
against.what_they_did: Utilities benefited from the existing normalization rule and had long defended it; no recorded congressional action by the industry on this bill is in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced utilities to give up excess deferred tax reserves accumulated when customers paid rates based on the old, higher corporate tax rate. Utilities' interest in keeping those reserves runs directly against customers' interest in getting them back.
